t: Introduction: topic and learning aim
n: In this lecture we consider the effect of high and low temperature. If high or low temperature acts on the whole body, heat stroke or general hypothermia results. If it acts on a part of the body, a burn or frostbite is produced. In a body found after a fire, it is necessary to establish whether the flame acted during life or after death. In assessing a burn, besides the degree, the area occupied by the injury is also important. It is determined approximately by the "rule of nines" and the "palm" rule. There are also signs of the effect of low temperature during life: the "posture of a frozen person" and haemorrhages in the stomach, that is, Vishnevskiy spots.

t: Normal body temperature and heat loss
n: First, on normal body temperature. Normally body temperature is 36–37 °C, and heat production and loss are regulated. If the temperature is below 22–25 °C or above 43–44 °C, changes incompatible with life occur in the tissues. The largest part of excess heat is shed by radiation, which is 55 %. Then 27 % by sweat and 15 % by conduction. Various excretions account for 3 %. That is, heat is lost mainly by radiation.

t: Types of effect of temperature
n: The effect of temperature is general or local. The general effect involves the whole organism, and as a result heat stroke or general hypothermia of the body develops. The local effect produces a burn or frostbite on a part of the body. The table shows that with high temperature the general effect is heat stroke and the local effect a thermal burn. With low temperature the general effect is general hypothermia and the local effect frostbite. Attention: in frostbite the body temperature is entirely normal, whereas in general hypothermia it falls.

t: Limits of body temperature (Iskandarov)
n: Now the limits of body temperature, according to Iskandarov. The organism keeps body temperature at 36–37 °C. Vital processes proceed within the range from +22 °C to +42–43 °C. If tissue temperature rises above +45–47 °C, proteins coagulate, enzyme activity is lost, and death occurs as a result of irreversible changes. When skin temperature exceeds +45–50 °C, a thermal burn is observed. Its depth depends on the temperature of the agent, the duration of action and the properties of the tissue. In boiling water a fourth-degree burn is not seen, since the water temperature does not exceed +100 °C and it cools quickly on reaching clothing and body.

t: Heat stroke: causes and mechanism
n: We consider the causes and mechanism of heat stroke. It occurs when a lot of heat is produced and little is lost. The cause is hot, humid air, no wind, a hot workshop and heavy physical work. Clothing that does not let air through, cardiovascular disease, obesity and old age increase predisposition. Children under one year are very sensitive. The main mechanism is haemodynamic disturbance: the blood thickens, circulation slows, tissue hyperthermia increases and hypoxia develops. In the stress reaction catecholamines and glucocorticoids are released. In the microcirculation stasis and vascular permeability are disturbed.

t: Acute and protracted forms of heat stroke
n: Heat stroke runs in an acute and a protracted form. In the acute form, in an unacclimatised organism consciousness is suddenly lost, coma develops and death occurs within a short time. The protracted form runs slowly, severity increases gradually, and three periods are distinguished. The first period is depression of the central nervous system, that is, the latent period. The second is excitation, restlessness. The third is prostration, coma and convulsions, with temperature above 41–42 °C. When body temperature exceeds 42–43 °C, death results from primary respiratory arrest.

t: Sunstroke and changes in the body
n: In sunstroke, when prolonged sunlight acts on the head, the central nervous system is disturbed: headache and clouding of consciousness are seen. Body temperature does not rise significantly. A first-degree burn, that is, erythema, may be present on the skin. The findings in the body are as follows. In the brain, congestion, oedema and petechial haemorrhages. In the internal organs, congestion and subserous haemorrhages. In the heart and lungs the blood is thick, and the lung is brown in colour. Rigor is rapid and strong, and the lividity is late and scanty. In death from heat stroke and sunstroke the morphological changes are similar, and there are no specific signs.

t: Quick question 1
n: Quick question: how does heat stroke differ from sunstroke, and can they be distinguished in the body? In heat stroke a lot of heat is produced and little is lost. Sunstroke, however, arises from heating of the head under the sun's rays without a head covering. A marked rise in body temperature is not typical of sunstroke, and signs of a first-degree burn, that is, erythema, may be present on the skin. Attention: heat stroke and sunstroke are not the same, but in the body the changes are similar and non-specific: cerebral congestion, rigor rapid and strong, lividity late and scanty.

t: Thermal burn: sources and factors of depth
n: A thermal burn begins when the temperature in the skin and underlying tissues exceeds 45–50 °C. The depth depends on the type of source, the temperature, the duration of action and the region. Sources: flame, tar, napalm, bitumen, water hotter than 60 °C, boiling steam, gases and a heated object. In areas of thin skin the burn is deeper. With hot liquid, hair and clothing are not damaged; the burn is superficial, in the form of streaks. With flame, hair and clothing are damaged, the burn is deep, and traces of soot are in the wound. Attention: a fourth-degree burn occurs only from the action of flame. A burn of the airways is characteristic of steam and hot gases.

t: Degrees of burn: comparison table
n: We compare the degrees of burn. First- and second-degree burns are regarded as superficial, and third- and fourth-degree burns as deep. In one injury different degrees often occur together, for example I–II or II–III. In first degree there is erythema, swelling and pain, and it passes without trace in 3–4 days. In second degree a serous blister forms and heals without scarring in 10–20 days; the floor of the blister is brown and firm, and no blood is discharged. In third degree there is necrosis and eschar, and granulation begins in the 2nd–3rd week. In fourth degree there is necrosis of the skin and deep tissues, and it forms only from flame. Attention: in III-A the necrosis is in the superficial layer, and in III-B there is complete necrosis of the epidermis and dermis.

t: Third- and fourth-degree burns and complications
n: Third- and fourth-degree burns and their complications. In third degree necrosis occurs: in III-A in the superficial layer, in III-B complete necrosis of the epidermis and dermis. In III-A there is granulation in the 2nd–3rd week, then a scar remains. In III-B an eschar remains, then a scar. In fourth degree the skin together with muscle, ligaments and bone undergoes necrosis. This degree occurs only from the action of flame. If there are different degrees in one injury, it is called a mixed burn, and it occurs in most cases. A deep burn often suppurates, heals slowly and leaves a coarse scar limiting the joints.

t: Determining the source of a burn: liquid and flame
n: From the features of a thermal burn the source of high temperature can be determined. A burn from hot liquid and one from flame differ in the hair, clothing, shape and depth of injury. With hot liquid, hair and clothing are not damaged, the injury takes the form of streaks, and the thermal burn is superficial. Liquid may run in under clothing. With flame, hair and clothing are damaged, the injury is tongue-shaped, and the burn is deep. In a flame burn, finding traces of soot in the wound is especially important for determining the source.

t: Heated object, steam and position at the time of the event
n: A heated object gives a deep burn with a circumscribed surface. The shape and size correspond to the contact surface of the object; this is a stamp-like or imprint burn. A burn of the airways is an injury characteristic only of steam and hot gases. From the location of the burn wounds one can form an opinion on the position of the victim at the time of the event. With hot liquid, the streaks are directed downward, that is, toward low-lying areas. With flame, however, the "tongues of flame" point upward, toward high-lying areas.

t: Case analysis: determining the source of a burn
n: Now the case analysis. Situation: the burn is superficial, in the form of streaks. Hair and clothing are not damaged, but skin covered by clothing is also burned. Hot liquid may run in under clothing. The streaks are directed toward the low-lying areas of the body. Attention: there is a risk of error. In a flame burn hair and clothing are damaged, the wound is tongue-shaped and deep, and traces of soot are found. Question: from which source, judging by these signs, is the burn, and in what position was the victim at the time of the event?

t: Burn area: the rule of nines
n: The rule of nines, A. Wallace, 1951, determines the burn area approximately. Head and neck 9 %, arm 9 %. Front and back of the trunk 18 % each. Thigh, and lower leg and foot, 9 % each. The perineum occupies 1 % of the body surface. In forensic assessment, besides the degree of the burn, the area occupied by the injury is also important.

t: The palm rule and special tables
n: By the palm rule, the area of the victim's palm makes up about 1 % of the total body surface. There are also special tables for determining the burn area, with which the burn surface is determined more precisely. A life-threatening burn: third to fourth degree over 10 %, third degree over 15 %, or second degree over 20 %. In the diagnosis the burn is written as a fraction: the area in the numerator, the degree in the denominator. For example: 10 % / II or 30 % (10 %) / II–III.

t: Criteria for a life-threatening burn
n: The danger of a burn to life is determined by its degree and by what part of the body surface it occupies. If a third- to fourth-degree burn occupies more than 10 % of the surface, a third-degree burn more than 15 %, and a second-degree burn more than 20 %, it is considered dangerous. If burn disease develops, a burn of smaller area also threatens life. If a burn of the airways runs with oedema and narrowing of the glottis, it is life-threatening.

t: Writing the burn in the diagnosis as a fraction
n: There is a procedure for writing a burn as a fraction in the diagnosis. The physician must state the degrees of the burn and the area occupied by each degree as fully as possible. In the numerator of the fraction, that is, at the top, the burn area is written in per cent. In the denominator, that is, below, the degrees of the burn are indicated. In brackets the area of the deeper burn is written. Examples: 10 % / II or 30 % (10 %) / II–III.

t: Burn area and prognosis (Iskandarov)
n: Iskandarov's data on area and prognosis. A first- to second-degree burn occupying less than 5 % of the body surface usually does not lead to death. In an extensive deep burn of more than 25 % of the body surface, even with modern treatment, 80–85 % of victims may die. According to most clinicians, with a deep burn of 45–50 % of the body surface the injury is incompatible with life. Burn disease develops when a second- to fourth-degree burn occupies more than 10–15 % of the body, or a first-degree burn 50 %. Toxaemia lasts 8–10 days.

t: Burn disease and its four periods
n: Burn disease consists of four periods. If a first-degree burn occupies more than 50 %, or second to fourth degree more than 10–15 % of the surface, and death does not occur at once, burn disease develops. The first period is shock, usually up to 1 day. The second is toxaemia, 1–2 weeks. The third is septicotoxaemia, with suppuration. The fourth is convalescence, that is, recovery. If burn of the airways and the effect of carbon monoxide are added, the probability of death rises two or more times. In children the disease is more severe, and in the elderly concomitant diseases aggravate the course.

t: Quick question 2: degree and area of burn
n: We test knowledge with quick questions. First question: into how many degrees is a thermal burn divided, and which degree occurs only from the action of flame? Answer: four; fourth degree only from flame. Second question: what percentage do the head and neck and the front of the trunk occupy in the "rule of nines"? Answer: 9 % and 18 %. Third question: by the "palm rule", what fraction of the body surface does the palm equal? Answer: about 1 %. Fourth question: name the four periods of burn disease. Answer: shock, toxaemia, septicotoxaemia and convalescence.

t: Case analysis: calculating the burn area
n: Now we calculate the burn area. This is a training example. A victim recovered from a fire has a third-degree burn of the head and neck, the front of the trunk and one arm. By the rule of nines, head and neck 9 %, front 18 %, arm 9 %. Total: 9 + 18 + 9 = 36 %. A third-degree burn of more than 15 % of the body surface is classed among injuries dangerous to life. Question: does this state meet the severity criterion? Write the diagnosis as a fraction: the area in the numerator, the degree in the denominator.

t: Vitality of the action of flame: the problem and soot
n: We turn to the problem of establishing the vitality of the action of flame. Victims of a fire often die of carbon monoxide poisoning, while the body is charred after death by the flame. The presence of soot in the airways, oesophagus and stomach shows that the flame acted during life. Soot may also be found in the cavities of the frontal and sphenoid bones, in vessels, in the cytoplasm of leucocytes and in Kupffer cells of the liver. Attention: with postmortem action of flame carboxyhaemoglobin does not exceed 20 %, whereas with exposure during life it may reach 60 %.

t: Carboxyhaemoglobin: action during life and after death
n: Finding carboxyhaemoglobin, that is, HbCO, in the blood and carboxymyoglobin in muscle is a sign of the action of flame during life. Blood is taken from the heart chambers and deep vessels, and the muscle sample from deep muscles. With action during life the HbCO concentration may reach 60 %. After death it does not exceed 20 %. Attention: HbCO may be found in superficial vessels even after death, so look at its amount.

t: The "crow's foot" and other signs of vitality
n: We continue with the signs of vitality. With action during life the eyeballs are usually not damaged. Above the eyelid fold there is a burn and soot, and at the bottom there is none. When the skin is stretched, the "crow's foot" sign is seen. Soot in the airways, oesophagus and stomach and a burn of the airways show that the flame acted during life. Abundant clotted blood in the heart and vessels, arterial thrombi in the injured area and fat embolism of the pulmonary vessels are also signs of vitality. In blisters of a burn during life the amount of protein is twice that in blisters formed after death.

t: Epidural haematoma and histological examination
n: In a body found after a fire there may be an epidural haematoma, and its origin must be distinguished. A traumatic haematoma is spindle-shaped and attached to the dura. A haematoma from the action of flame is crescent-shaped and not attached to the dura. In establishing vitality, external injuries and the results of histological examination of the internal organs are of great importance. Therefore microscopic examination of the skin, soft tissues and internal organs is necessary.

t: The pugilistic attitude and the burning time of the body
n: Under the action of flame, moisture in the body evaporates, proteins coagulate, and the muscles become dense and shortened. Therefore the limbs flex and the "pugilistic attitude" forms; it is seen in complete charring of the body. The skin covering also becomes dense. If the action on different areas of the body is unequal, cracks and splits may appear in the skin. The body of an infant burns to ash in 2–3 hours, an adult's in about 20 hours. In a gas crematorium less than an hour is needed.

t: Burning time of the body: differences between sources
n: The burning time of a body differs in the sources. Ignatovsky, 1910, gave 40–50 hours, and Rayskiy, 1953, 10–20 hours. According to Giyosov, an infant's body burns to ash in 2–3 hours, an adult's in about 20 hours, and in a gas crematorium less than an hour. Iskandarov: in a special investigation an adult's body burned in 4–4.5 hours, and in a crematorium in less than 1 hour. The times depend on the conditions of burning, so the expert compares the burning time with the conditions given.

t: Signs of vitality of a burn (Iskandarov)
n: Signs of vitality of a burn according to Iskandarov. A reliable sign of life at the seat of a fire is carboxyhaemoglobin in the blood and soot in the airways, oesophagus and stomach. During life soot is found in the smallest bronchi and alveoli, sometimes in the frontal sinus, in the cardiovascular system and in the Kupffer cells of the liver. In the mucosa of the airways there are congestion, oedema, haemorrhages and whitish foci of necrosis. A sign is also non-injury in the folds of the face. Total protein in a blister of a burn during life is 4.2–4.9 %, about 2 times the protein in a blister after death. Fat embolism of the lungs also occurs.

t: Case analysis: a body found after a fire
n: Case analysis. A charred body was recovered from the seat of a fire. In a fire death often results from carbon monoxide poisoning, and the body is then charred. If soot is in the airways, oesophagus and stomach, the flame acted during life. Soot may also be found in the vessels and leucocytes. Attention: with postmortem action of flame, carboxyhaemoglobin is also present in the superficial vessels, but does not exceed 20 %. During life it reaches 60 %. The "crow's foot" on the skin of the eyelids and a twofold excess of protein in the burn blisters also show action during life. Question: which signs will you look for?

t: Low temperature: factors and general effect
n: Now we turn to the effect of low temperature. The effect of low temperature is intensified by cold, high humidity and wind. In almost all cases it is the result of an accident. Predisposing factors: clothing unsuited to the season, fatigue, hunger, illness, immobility and intoxication. Children and the elderly are especially sensitive. With prolonged exposure, general hypothermia may develop even at an air temperature of up to +10 °C. Alcohol dilates the skin vessels and increases heat loss. In air, death usually occurs within a few hours, in cold water in 1–1.5 hours. On sudden entry, death is possible from vascular collapse or shock.

t: Stages of general hypothermia
n: General hypothermia develops in stages. The first stage is compensation: the organism increases metabolism and tries to keep body temperature normal. The second is decompensation. In the third the temperature falls to +30…+28 °C and the cortex is disturbed. Each fall of 1 °C slows biochemical processes about 2 times. In the fourth, final stage the temperature is +25…+22 °C. The fifth is death, most often from primary respiratory arrest.

t: External signs of general hypothermia
n: External signs of general hypothermia. In the posture of a frozen person the arms are flexed to the chest and the legs to the abdomen. The posture reduces the surface of heat loss, though in severe intoxication it may be absent. Rayskiy's signs: ice in the mouth and nose, hoar frost on the eyelashes. Puparev's sign: the testicle is contracted and the scrotum drawn up. Cadaveric lividity at sub-zero temperature is pinkish-red. At above-zero temperature, up to +10 °C, the lividity is bluish-violet, since the tissues have time to use up the oxygen. A layer of ice under snow is not specific: it forms also when a body that has not cooled is laid on snow.

t: Internal signs and Vishnevskiy spots
n: Internal signs. In the blood and organs there is congestion, and bright scarlet clotted blood is found. Pukhnarevich's sign: the stomach is empty and small. Fabrikantov's sign: small haemorrhages in the renal pelvis. Vishnevskiy spots in the gastric mucosa, up to 0.5 cm, occur in 80–90 % of deaths and may be detected even after 6–9 months. If death is rapid, the spots are scanty or absent, and in children they are often absent. If after several hours, the spots are numerous. Kasyanov's sign is a change in the epithelium of the straight tubules of the kidney, and in histochemistry glycogen disappears.

t: Quick question 3: signs of general hypothermia
n: Quick question: what are the small haemorrhages in the gastric mucosa in those who died of general hypothermia called, and in what proportion of cases do they occur? Answer: S. M. Vishnevskiy spots. They are seen in 80–90 % of deaths from hypothermia. The spots lie on the crests of the mucosal folds, up to 0.5 cm in diameter. They are easily removed with the back of a knife or a stream of water, and may be detected even 6–9 months after death. Attention: if death occurs quickly, the spots may be very few or absent altogether, and in young children they are often not seen.

t: The frozen body and the difference from signs of life
n: Freezing of the body differs from signs of life. On freezing, the volume of the brain and parenchymatous organs increases, and there is no serious change in the thoracic and abdominal cavities. In the cranium, freezing of the brain leads to fractures of the bones, separation of the sutures and rupture of the soft tissues from within. Thawing takes several days. If warm air or water up to +50 °C is used, haemolysis and imbibition are marked. During life, under the effect of low temperature, there are spasm, oedema and petechial haemorrhages. After death, however, multiple small cracks and detachment of the epidermis are observed. A layer of ice under snow also appears on a body that has not cooled.

t: Case analysis: death from general hypothermia
n: Case analysis. A body found in an open place has the arms flexed to the chest and the legs flexed to the abdomen. There is hoar frost on the eyebrows and eyelashes, and icicles near the nose. On internal examination the organs are congested, in the left heart and aorta there is bright scarlet clotted blood, the stomach is empty, and there are small haemorrhages in its mucosa. Question: which signs indicate the effect of low temperature during life, and what colour is the lividity expected to be? Attention: a layer of ice under snow is not specific, and in severe intoxication the "posture of a frozen person" may be absent.

t: Frostbite and its degrees
n: Now frostbite and its degrees. The latent period corresponds to the time when the temperature in the tissue is lowered. The reactive period begins after warming. In the reactive period, four degrees of frostbite are distinguished according to the depth of injury. In first degree the skin is reddish-bluish and slightly swollen, passing in 3–7 days. In second degree there are blisters with clear fluid, 10–20 days, without scarring. In third degree there is necrosis of the skin and haemorrhagic blisters, 1–2 months or longer, and a scar remains. In fourth degree there is necrosis down to the bone and a demarcation rim, with a scar after weeks or months. After first and second degree heal, the site of injury remains very sensitive to cold for a long time.

t: Frostbite: area, severity and repercussion
n: Frostbite is most often an accident and occurs on the fingertips and toes, ear, nose and cheek. On the foot the first toe is more often injured, on the hand the third and fourth fingers. The repercussion phenomenon: when one arm or leg is frostbitten, local changes may develop also on the opposite side, which was not exposed. In the medical document it is important to record the circumstances of the event, the lowering of local temperature in the injured area, the degree of frostbite and the area of injury. Life-threatening: third to fourth degree over 10 % of the body surface, third degree over 15 %, or second degree over 20 %.

t: Conclusion: algorithm for establishing vitality and area
n: Conclusion and algorithm for establishing vitality and area. The area of a thermal burn is assessed by the rule of nines: head and neck 9 %, arm 9 %, front 18 %, back 18 %, thigh 9 %, lower leg and foot 9 %, perineum 1 %. The palm is about 1 %. In the action of flame during life, there is soot in the airways, oesophagus and stomach. Carboxyhaemoglobin after death does not exceed 20 %, during life it is up to 60 %. The "crow's foot" sign and non-injury of the eyeball show action during life, and in blisters formed during life there is twice as much protein. Attention: a spindle-shaped epidural haematoma attached to the dura is trauma. A crescent-shaped, unattached haematoma is the postmortem action of flame.
